title: Oxygen use of a mouse and a lizard across temperatures

stimulus.title: Oxygen consumption of a mouse and a lizard at different air temperatures
stimulus.text: Researchers measured the rate of oxygen consumption of six deer mice (an endotherm) and six fence lizards (an ectotherm), each with a body mass of about 20 g. Each animal was fasted for 6 hours and then rested alone in a sealed chamber kept at one air temperature for 1 hour while O₂ use was measured. Each animal was tested at all seven temperatures, in random order, on different days.

table.caption: Rate of O₂ consumption (mL of O₂ per g of body mass per hour, mean ± 2 SE, n = 6)

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how an endotherm such as the mouse keeps its body temperature nearly constant when the air around it cools.

rubric.point: Describes that the endotherm increases heat production from its own metabolism (cellular respiration; shivering or burning fat) as the air cools, balancing the greater heat loss (negative feedback). Accept added mention of insulation or reduced blood flow to the skin.
accept: it raises its metabolic rate, making more heat by cellular respiration
it shivers or burns more fat to generate heat, making up for faster heat loss
negative feedback: a drop in body temperature triggers more heat production

parts.sample: When the air cools, the mouse loses heat faster. Sensors detect the drop, and the mouse responds by raising its metabolic rate, shivering and burning more fat, so its cellular respiration releases more heat and body temperature stays near its set point. This is negative feedback.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt:
(i) Identify the independent variable in the experiment.
(ii) Justify fasting each animal for 6 hours before it was measured.
(iii) State the null hypothesis for comparing the mouse's rate of O₂ consumption at 30 °C and at 35 °C.

rubric.point: (i) The air temperature in the chamber (accept: temperature and kind of animal).
accept: air temperature
the temperature of the chamber
temperature (5 to 35 °C)

rubric.point: (ii) Digesting a meal raises metabolic rate (O₂ use), so fasting makes sure differences in O₂ use come from temperature, not from recent feeding; it controls a variable that would otherwise differ between trials.
accept: digestion uses energy and raises O₂ consumption, so fasting removes that effect
keeps food in the gut from affecting the measurement
so every animal is in the same resting, post-absorptive state

rubric.point: (iii) There is no difference in the mean rate of O₂ consumption of the mice at 30 °C and at 35 °C (air temperature in this range has no effect).
accept: mean O₂ use at 30 °C equals mean O₂ use at 35 °C
temperature between 30 and 35 °C does not affect the mice's oxygen consumption
any difference between the two means is due to chance

parts.sample: (i) The air temperature in the chamber. (ii) Digesting food raises an animal's metabolic rate and O₂ use. Fasting every animal for the same time means the measured O₂ use reflects temperature, not how recently it ate. (iii) Null hypothesis: there is no difference between the mean O₂ consumption of the mice at 30 °C and at 35 °C.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt:
(i) Calculate how many times greater the mouse's rate of O₂ consumption is than the lizard's at 20 °C. Show your work.
(ii) Using the error bars (± 2 SE), determine whether the mouse's rate of O₂ consumption differs between 30 °C and 35 °C, and justify your answer.

accept: about 23 times greater

rubric.point: (ii) No clear difference: the intervals 2.3-2.9 and 2.2-2.8 mL per g per hour overlap (the means differ by less than the error bars), so the null hypothesis is not rejected.
accept: the error bars overlap, so the difference is not significant
2.6 ± 0.3 and 2.5 ± 0.3 overlap, so they do not differ
no difference; the ±2 SE ranges overlap

parts.sample: (i) 4.4 ÷ 0.19 = 23. At 20 °C the mouse uses about 23 times as much O₂ per gram as the lizard. (ii) They do not clearly differ. At 30 °C the interval is 2.3-2.9 and at 35 °C it is 2.2-2.8 mL per g per hour; the intervals overlap, so the small difference in means could be due to chance.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt:
(i) Explain why the mouse's rate of O₂ consumption rises as the air temperature falls from 30 °C to 5 °C.
(ii) Explain why the lizard's rate of O₂ consumption rises as the air temperature rises.
(iii) Both animals live where the air is about 10 °C. Predict which animal must eat more food per gram of body mass each day to keep its body mass steady, and about how many times more, and justify your prediction using the data.

rubric.point: (i) Below about 30 °C the mouse loses heat faster, so it makes more heat by cellular respiration to hold its body temperature; respiration uses O₂, so O₂ use rises.
accept: more cellular respiration is needed to make heat as heat loss increases
the mouse burns more fuel to stay warm, which uses more oxygen
colder air means more heat lost, so metabolic heat production and O₂ use go up

rubric.point: (ii) The lizard's body temperature follows the air temperature; warmer cells have faster enzyme-catalyzed reactions, so its metabolic rate and O₂ use rise.
accept: as an ectotherm its body warms with the air, speeding up enzyme reactions
higher body temperature increases the rate of cellular respiration
metabolism speeds up with temperature because molecules move faster and enzymes work faster

rubric.point: (iii) Predicts that the mouse must eat more, roughly 80 times as much per gram (6.3 ÷ 0.08 ≈ 79; accept 70-80 or "tens of times"), justified by its much higher O₂ consumption: O₂ use measures the rate of cellular respiration, which burns food, so the mouse uses food energy far faster.
accept: the mouse, about 79 times more, because it uses 6.3 vs 0.08 mL O₂ per g per hour
the mouse: its O₂ use, and so its use of food energy, is about 80 times the lizard's at 10 °C
the mouse, because O₂ consumption tracks how fast food is burned, and it is far higher for the mouse

parts.sample: (i) As the air gets colder, the mouse loses heat faster. To keep its body near 37 °C it raises its rate of cellular respiration to release more heat, and respiration uses O₂, so O₂ consumption rises. (ii) The lizard's body temperature follows the air. In warmer cells, enzyme-catalyzed reactions, including those of respiration, run faster, so its metabolic rate and O₂ use rise. (iii) The mouse must eat more: about 6.3 ÷ 0.08 ≈ 79 times as much per gram each day. O₂ consumption measures how fast cellular respiration burns food, and at 10 °C the mouse burns food about 79 times as fast as the lizard, mostly to make heat, so it must replace that food to keep its mass steady.
